L42: /*
L43:  * Timestamp structure for the timestamps in struct statx.
L44:  *
L45:  * tv_sec holds the number of seconds before (negative) or after (positive)
L46:  * 00:00:00 1st January 1970 UTC.
L47:  *
L48:  * tv_nsec holds a number of nanoseconds (0..999,999,999) after the tv_sec time.
L49:  *
L50:  * __reserved is held in case we need a yet finer resolution.
L51:  */
L52: struct statx_timestamp {
L53: 	__s64	tv_sec;
L54: 	__u32	tv_nsec;
L55: 	__s32	__reserved;
L56: };
L57: /*
L58:  * Structures for the extended file attribute retrieval system call
L59:  * (statx()).
L60:  *
L61:  * The caller passes a mask of what they're specifically interested in as a
L62:  * parameter to statx().  What statx() actually got will be indicated in
L63:  * st_mask upon return.
L64:  *
L65:  * For each bit in the mask argument:
L66:  *
L67:  * - if the datum is not supported:
L68:  *
L69:  *   - the bit will be cleared, and
L70:  *
L71:  *   - the datum will be set to an appropriate fabricated value if one is
L72:  *     available (eg. CIFS can take a default uid and gid), otherwise
L73:  *
L74:  *   - the field will be cleared;
L75:  *
L76:  * - otherwise, if explicitly requested:
L77:  *
L78:  *   - the datum will be synchronised to the server if AT_STATX_FORCE_SYNC is
L79:  *     set or if the datum is considered out of date, and
L80:  *
L81:  *   - the field will be filled in and the bit will be set;
L82:  *
L83:  * - otherwise, if not requested, but available in approximate form without any
L84:  *   effort, it will be filled in anyway, and the bit will be set upon return
L85:  *   (it might not be up to date, however, and no attempt will be made to
L86:  *   synchronise the internal state first);
L87:  *
L88:  * - otherwise the field and the bit will be cleared before returning.
L89:  *
L90:  * Items in STATX_BASIC_STATS may be marked unavailable on return, but they
L91:  * will have values installed for compatibility purposes so that stat() and
L92:  * co. can be emulated in userspace.
L93:  */
L94: struct statx {
L95: 	/* 0x00 */
L96: 	/* What results were written [uncond] */
L97: 	__u32	stx_mask;
L98: 	/* Preferred general I/O size [uncond] */
L99: 	__u32	stx_blksize;
L100: 
L101: 	/* Flags conveying information about the file [uncond] */
L102: 	__u64	stx_attributes;
L103: 
L104: 	/* 0x10 */
L105: 	/* Number of hard links */
L106: 	__u32	stx_nlink;
L107: 
L108: 	/* User ID of owner */
L109: 	__u32	stx_uid;
L110: 
L111: 	/* Group ID of owner */
L112: 	__u32	stx_gid;
L113: 
L114: 	/* File mode */
L115: 	__u16	stx_mode;
L116: 	__u16	__spare0[1];
L117: 
L118: 	/* 0x20 */
L119: 	/* Inode number */
L120: 	__u64	stx_ino;
L121: 
L122: 	/* File size */
L123: 	__u64	stx_size;
L124: 
L125: 	/* Number of 512-byte blocks allocated */
L126: 	__u64	stx_blocks;
L127: 	/* Mask to show what's supported in stx_attributes */
L128: 	__u64	stx_attributes_mask;
L129: 
L130: 	/* 0x40 */
L131: 	/* Last access time */
L132: 	struct statx_timestamp	stx_atime;
L133: 
L134: 	/* File creation time */
L135: 	struct statx_timestamp	stx_btime;
L136: 
L137: 	/* Last attribute change time */
L138: 	struct statx_timestamp	stx_ctime;
L139: 
L140: 	/* Last data modification time */
L141: 	struct statx_timestamp	stx_mtime;
L142: 
L143: 	/* 0x80 */
L144: 	/* Device ID of special file [if bdev/cdev] */
L145: 	__u32	stx_rdev_major;
L146: 	__u32	stx_rdev_minor;
L147: 	/* ID of device containing file [uncond] */
L148: 	__u32	stx_dev_major;
L149: 	__u32	stx_dev_minor;
L150: 
L151: 	/* 0x90 */
L152: 	__u64	stx_mnt_id;
L153: 
L154: 	/* Memory buffer alignment for direct I/O */
L155: 	__u32	stx_dio_mem_align;
L156: 
L157: 	/* File offset alignment for direct I/O */
L158: 	__u32	stx_dio_offset_align;
L159: 
L160: 	/* 0xa0 */
L161: 	/* Subvolume identifier */
L162: 	__u64	stx_subvol;
L163: 
L164: 	/* Min atomic write unit in bytes */
L165: 	__u32	stx_atomic_write_unit_min;
L166: 
L167: 	/* Max atomic write unit in bytes */
L168: 	__u32	stx_atomic_write_unit_max;
L169: 	/* 0xb0 */
L170: 	/* Max atomic write segment count */
L171: 	__u32   stx_atomic_write_segments_max;
L172: 
L173: 	/* File offset alignment for direct I/O reads */
L174: 	__u32	stx_dio_read_offset_align;
L175: 
L176: 	/* Optimised max atomic write unit in bytes */
L177: 	__u32	stx_atomic_write_unit_max_opt;
L178: 	__u32	__spare2[1];
L179: 
L180: 	/* 0xc0 */
L181: 	__u64	__spare3[8];	/* Spare space for future expansion */
L182: 
L183: 	/* 0x100 */
L184: };
L185: /*
L186:  * Flags to be stx_mask
L187:  *
L188:  * Query request/result mask for statx() and struct statx::stx_mask.
L189:  *
L190:  * These bits should be set in the mask argument of statx() to request
L191:  * particular items when calling statx().
L192:  */
L193: #define STATX_TYPE		0x00000001U	/* Want/got stx_mode & S_IFMT */
L194: #define STATX_MODE		0x00000002U	/* Want/got stx_mode & ~S_IFMT */
L195: #define STATX_NLINK		0x00000004U	/* Want/got stx_nlink */
L196: #define STATX_UID		0x00000008U	/* Want/got stx_uid */
L197: #define STATX_GID		0x00000010U	/* Want/got stx_gid */
L198: #define STATX_ATIME		0x00000020U	/* Want/got stx_atime */
L199: #define STATX_MTIME		0x00000040U	/* Want/got stx_mtime */
L200: #define STATX_CTIME		0x00000080U	/* Want/got stx_ctime */
L201: #define STATX_INO		0x00000100U	/* Want/got stx_ino */
L202: #define STATX_SIZE		0x00000200U	/* Want/got stx_size */
L203: #define STATX_BLOCKS		0x00000400U	/* Want/got stx_blocks */
L204: #define STATX_BASIC_STATS	0x000007ffU	/* The stuff in the normal stat struct */
L205: #define STATX_BTIME		0x00000800U	/* Want/got stx_btime */
L206: #define STATX_MNT_ID		0x00001000U	/* Got stx_mnt_id */
L207: #define STATX_DIOALIGN		0x00002000U	/* Want/got direct I/O alignment info */
L208: #define STATX_MNT_ID_UNIQUE	0x00004000U	/* Want/got extended stx_mount_id */
L209: #define STATX_SUBVOL		0x00008000U	/* Want/got stx_subvol */
L210: #define STATX_WRITE_ATOMIC	0x00010000U	/* Want/got atomic_write_* fields */
L211: #define STATX_DIO_READ_ALIGN	0x00020000U	/* Want/got dio read alignment info */
L212: #define STATX__RESERVED		0x80000000U	/* Reserved for future struct statx expansion */
L213: #ifndef __KERNEL__
L214: /*
L215:  * This is deprecated, and shall remain the same value in the future.  To avoid
L216:  * confusion please use the equivalent (STATX_BASIC_STATS | STATX_BTIME)
L217:  * instead.
L218:  */
L219: #define STATX_ALL		0x00000fffU
L220: #endif
L221: /*
L222:  * Attributes to be found in stx_attributes and masked in stx_attributes_mask.
L223:  *
L224:  * These give information about the features or the state of a file that might
L225:  * be of use to ordinary userspace programs such as GUIs or ls rather than
L226:  * specialised tools.
L227:  *
L228:  * Note that the flags marked [I] correspond to the FS_IOC_SETFLAGS flags
L229:  * semantically.  Where possible, the numerical value is picked to correspond
L230:  * also.  Note that the DAX attribute indicates that the file is in the CPU
L231:  * direct access state.  It does not correspond to the per-inode flag that
L232:  * some filesystems support.
L233:  *
L234:  */
L235: #define STATX_ATTR_COMPRESSED		0x00000004 /* [I] File is compressed by the fs */
L236: #define STATX_ATTR_IMMUTABLE		0x00000010 /* [I] File is marked immutable */
L237: #define STATX_ATTR_APPEND		0x00000020 /* [I] File is append-only */
L238: #define STATX_ATTR_NODUMP		0x00000040 /* [I] File is not to be dumped */
L239: #define STATX_ATTR_ENCRYPTED		0x00000800 /* [I] File requires key to decrypt in fs */
L240: #define STATX_ATTR_AUTOMOUNT		0x00001000 /* Dir: Automount trigger */
L241: #define STATX_ATTR_MOUNT_ROOT		0x00002000 /* Root of a mount */
L242: #define STATX_ATTR_VERITY		0x00100000 /* [I] Verity protected file */
L243: #define STATX_ATTR_DAX			0x00200000 /* File is currently in DAX state */
L244: #define STATX_ATTR_WRITE_ATOMIC		0x00400000 /* File supports atomic write operations */
L245: #endif /* _UAPI_LINUX_STAT_H */

L9:     PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER(2const)             PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER(2const)
L10: ## NAME         cite12†top L11: 
L12:            PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER - set/unset the "child subreaper" attribute
L13:            of the calling process
L14: 
L15: 
L16: ## LIBRARY         cite12†top L17: 
L18:            Standard C library (libc, -lc)
L19: 
L20: 
L21: ## SYNOPSIS         cite12†top L22: 
L23:            #include <linux/prctl.h>  /* Definition of PR_* constants */
L24:            #include <sys/prctl.h>
L25: 
L26:            int prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, long set);
L27: ## DESCRIPTION         cite12†top L28: 
L29:            If set is nonzero, set the "child subreaper" attribute of the
L30:            calling process; if set is zero, unset the attribute.
L31: 
L32:            A subreaper fulfills the role of cite13†init(1) for its descendant
L33:            processes.  When a process becomes orphaned (i.e., its immediate
L34:            parent terminates), then that process will be reparented to the
L35:            nearest still living ancestor subreaper.  Subsequently, calls to
L36:            cite14†getppid(2) in the orphaned process will now return the PID of the
L37:            subreaper process, and when the orphan terminates, it is the
L38:            subreaper process that will receive a SIGCHLD signal and will be
L39:            able to cite15†wait(2) on the process to discover its termination status.
L40: 
L41:            The setting of the "child subreaper" attribute is not inherited by
L42:            children created by cite16†fork(2) and cite17†clone(2) .  The setting is
L43:            preserved across cite18†execve(2) .
L44: 
L45:            Establishing a subreaper process is useful in session management
L46:            frameworks where a hierarchical group of processes is managed by a
L47:            subreaper process that needs to be informed when one of the
L48:            processes—for example, a double-forked daemon—terminates (perhaps
L49:            so that it can restart that process).  Some cite13†init(1) frameworks
L50:            (e.g., cite19†systemd(1) ) employ a subreaper process for similar reasons.
L51: ## RETURN VALUE         cite12†top L52: 
L53:            On success, 0 is returned.  On error, -1 is returned, and cite20†errno is
L54:            set to indicate the error.
L55: 
L56:

L6: cite3†NAME | cite4†LIBRARY | cite5†SYNOPSIS | cite6†DESCRIPTION | cite7†RETURN VALUE | cite8†ERRORS | cite9†VERSIONS | cite10†STANDARDS | cite11†HISTORY | cite12†NOTES | cite13†BUGS | cite14†EXAMPLES | cite15†SEE ALSO | cite16†COLOPHON L7: [Input] [Input] [Input]  |

L9:     wait(2)                    System Calls Manual                    wait(2)
L10: ## NAME         cite17†top L11: 
L12:            wait, waitpid, waitid - wait for process to change state
L13: 
L14: 
L15: ## LIBRARY         cite17†top L16: 
L17:            Standard C library (libc, -lc)
L18: ## SYNOPSIS         cite17†top L19: 
L20:            #include <sys/wait.h>
L21: 
L22:            pid_t wait(int *_Nullable wstatus);
L23:            pid_t waitpid(pid_t pid, int *_Nullable wstatus, int options);
L24: 
L25:            int waitid(idtype_t idtype, id_t id, siginfo_t *infop, int options);
L26:                            /* This is the glibc and POSIX interface; see
L27:                               VERSIONS for information on the raw system call.  */
L28: 
L29:        Feature Test Macro Requirements for glibc (see
L30:        cite18†feature_test_macros(7) ):
L31: 
L32:            waitid():
L33:                Since glibc 2.26:
L34:                    _XOPEN_SOURCE >= 500 || _POSIX_C_SOURCE >= 200809L
L35:                glibc 2.25 and earlier:
L36:                    _XOPEN_SOURCE
L37:                        || /* Since glibc 2.12: */ _POSIX_C_SOURCE >= 200809L
L38:                        || /* glibc <= 2.19: */ _BSD_SOURCE
L39: ## DESCRIPTION         cite17†top L40: 
L41:            All of these system calls are used to wait for state changes in a
L42:            child of the calling process, and obtain information about the
L43:            child whose state has changed.  A state change is considered to
L44:            be: the child terminated; the child was stopped by a signal; or
L45:            the child was resumed by a signal.  In the case of a terminated
L46:            child, performing a wait allows the system to release the
L47:            resources associated with the child; if a wait is not performed,
L48:            then the terminated child remains in a "zombie" state (see NOTES
L49:            below).
L50: 
L51:            If a child has already changed state, then these calls return
L52:            immediately.  Otherwise, they block until either a child changes
L53:            state or a signal handler interrupts the call (assuming that
L54:            system calls are not automatically restarted using the SA_RESTART
L55:            flag of cite19†sigaction(2) ).  In the remainder of this page, a child
L56:            whose state has changed and which has not yet been waited upon by
L57:            one of these system calls is termed waitable.
L58: 
L59:        wait() and waitpid()
L60:            The wait() system call suspends execution of the calling thread
L61:            until one of its children terminates.  The call wait(&wstatus) is
L62:            equivalent to:
L63: 
L64:                waitpid(-1, &wstatus, 0);
L65:            The waitpid() system call suspends execution of the calling thread
L66:            until a child specified by pid argument has changed state.  By
L67:            default, waitpid() waits only for terminated children, but this
L68:            behavior is modifiable via the options argument, as described
L69:            below.
L70: 
L71:            The value of pid can be:
L72: 
L73:            < -1   meaning wait for any child process whose process group ID
L74:                   is equal to the absolute value of pid.
L75:            -1     meaning wait for any child process.
L76: 
L77:            0      meaning wait for any child process whose process group ID
L78:                   is equal to that of the calling process at the time of the
L79:                   call to waitpid().
L80: 
L81:            > 0    meaning wait for the child whose process ID is equal to the
L82:                   value of pid.
L83: 
L84:            The value of options is an OR of zero or more of the following
L85:            constants:
L86: 
L87:            WNOHANG
L88:                   return immediately if no child has exited.
L89: 
L90:            WUNTRACED
L91:                   also return if a child has stopped (but not traced via
L92:                   cite20†ptrace(2) ).  Status for traced children which have stopped
L93:                   is provided even if this option is not specified.
L94: 
L95:            WCONTINUED (since Linux 2.6.10)
L96:                   also return if a stopped child has been resumed by delivery
L97:                   of SIGCONT.
L98:            (For Linux-only options, see below.)
L99: 
L100:            If wstatus is not NULL, wait() and waitpid() store status
L101:            information in the int to which it points.  This integer can be
L102:            inspected with the following macros (which take the integer itself
L103:            as an argument, not a pointer to it, as is done in wait() and
L104:            waitpid()!):
L105: 
L106:            WIFEXITED(wstatus)
L107:                   returns true if the child terminated normally, that is, by
L108:                   calling cite21†exit(3) or cite22†_exit(2) , or by returning from main().
L109: 
L110:            WEXITSTATUS(wstatus)
L111:                   returns the exit status of the child.  This consists of the
L112:                   least significant 8 bits of the status argument that the
L113:                   child specified in a call to cite21†exit(3) or cite22†_exit(2) or as the
L114:                   argument for a return statement in main().  This macro
L115:                   should be employed only if WIFEXITED returned true.
L116:            WIFSIGNALED(wstatus)
L117:                   returns true if the child process was terminated by a
L118:                   signal.
L119: 
L120:            WTERMSIG(wstatus)
L121:                   returns the number of the signal that caused the child
L122:                   process to terminate.  This macro should be employed only
L123:                   if WIFSIGNALED returned true.
L124: 
L125:            WCOREDUMP(wstatus)  // POSIX.1-2024
L126:                   returns true if the child produced a core dump (see
L127:                   cite23†core(5) ).  This macro should be employed only if
L128:                   WIFSIGNALED returned true.
L129: 
L130:            WIFSTOPPED(wstatus)  // POSIX.1-2024
L131:                   returns true if the child process was stopped by delivery
L132:                   of a signal; this is possible only if the call was done
L133:                   using WUNTRACED or when the child is being traced (see
L134:                   cite20†ptrace(2) ).
L135: 
L136:            WSTOPSIG(wstatus)
L137:                   returns the number of the signal which caused the child to
L138:                   stop.  This macro should be employed only if WIFSTOPPED
L139:                   returned true.
L140: 
L141:            WIFCONTINUED(wstatus)
L142:                   (since Linux 2.6.10) returns true if the child process was
L143:                   resumed by delivery of SIGCONT.
L144: 
L145:        waitid()
L146:            The waitid() system call (available since Linux 2.6.9) provides
L147:            more precise control over which child state changes to wait for.
L148: 
L149:            The idtype and id arguments select the child(ren) to wait for, as
L150:            follows:
L151: 
L152:            idtype == P_PID
L153:                   Wait for the child whose process ID matches id.
L154: 
L155:            idtype == P_PIDFD (since Linux 5.4)
L156:                   Wait for the child referred to by the PID file descriptor
L157:                   specified in id.  (See cite24†pidfd_open(2) for further
L158:                   information on PID file descriptors.)
L159: 
L160:            idtype == P_PGID
L161:                   Wait for any child whose process group ID matches id.
L162:                   Since Linux 5.4, if id is zero, then wait for any child
L163:                   that is in the same process group as the caller's process
L164:                   group at the time of the call.
L165: 
L166:            idtype == P_ALL
L167:                   Wait for any child; id is ignored.
L168:            The child state changes to wait for are specified by ORing one or
L169:            more of the following flags in options:
L170: 
L171:            WEXITED
L172:                   Wait for children that have terminated.
L173: 
L174:            WSTOPPED
L175:                   Wait for children that have been stopped by delivery of a
L176:                   signal.
L177: 
L178:            WCONTINUED
L179:                   Wait for (previously stopped) children that have been
L180:                   resumed by delivery of SIGCONT.
L181:            The following flags may additionally be ORed in options:
L182: 
L183:            WNOHANG
L184:                   As for waitpid().
L185: 
L186:            WNOWAIT
L187:                   Leave the child in a waitable state; a later wait call can
L188:                   be used to again retrieve the child status information.
L189: 
L190:            Upon successful return, waitid() fills in the following fields of
L191:            the siginfo_t structure pointed to by infop:
L192: 
L193:            si_pid The process ID of the child.
L194:            si_uid The real user ID of the child.  (This field is not set on
L195:                   most other implementations.)
L196: 
L197:            si_signo
L198:                   Always set to SIGCHLD.
L199: 
L200:            si_status
L201:                   Either the exit status of the child, as given to cite22†_exit(2) L202:                   (or cite21†exit(3) ), or the signal that caused the child to
L203:                   terminate, stop, or continue.  The si_code field can be
L204:                   used to determine how to interpret this field.
L205: 
L206:            si_code
L207:                   Set to one of: CLD_EXITED (child called cite22†_exit(2) );
L208:                   CLD_KILLED (child killed by signal); CLD_DUMPED (child
L209:                   killed by signal, and dumped core); CLD_STOPPED (child
L210:                   stopped by signal); CLD_TRAPPED (traced child has trapped);
L211:                   or CLD_CONTINUED (child continued by SIGCONT).
L212:

L214:            a waitable state, then waitid() returns 0 immediately and the
